working: One-one: f(p) = f(q) gives (p-m)(q-n) = (q-m)(p-n), which reduces to (p-q)(m-n) = 0, so p = q since m != n. Onto: solving y = (x-m)/(x-n) gives x = (yn-m)/(y-1), undefined at y = 1, so 1 is never attained and the range is R minus {1}, a proper subset of the codomain. Hence one-one into.
subtopic: Function Definition and Classification — Injectivity, Surjectivity, Bijectivity
notes: Minor stem defect, not answer-affecting: f is declared R -> R but is undefined at x = n, so the domain should read R minus {n}. The injectivity/surjectivity verdict is unchanged either way.

working: (h o (g o f))(x) = h(g(f(x))) = log_e(tan(x^2)). At x = sqrt(pi/2) we get x^2 = pi/2 and tan(pi/2) is undefined (it diverges to +inf from the left and -inf from the right), so log_e(tan(x^2)) has no value there. None of 0, 1, 2 is the value, so 'None of these' is what the stem as printed supports.
notes: Answered AS PRINTED, not repaired. The composite is undefined at the given point because tan(pi/2) does not exist, so D is the only tenable option. The standard textbook version of this question uses x = sqrt(pi/4), where tan(pi/4) = 1 and log_e(1) = 0, i.e. option A; if the printed key is A, the likely cause is a pi/4 -> pi/2 corruption in the stem rather than a wrong key. working: (g o f)(x) = g(f(x)) = g(x^2) = sin(x^2), which is option B as printed (sin x^2). Option D (sin x) would be f o g misread and options A/C are unrelated.
Set y = 4x + 3 and solve for x: x = (y - 3)/4. Since Y is exactly the image of N under f, this is the inverse, so g(y) = (y-3)/4. Check: g(f(x)) = (4x+3-3)/4 = x.

(A - B) U (A - C) = (A n B') U (A n C') = A n (B' U C') = A n (B n C)' by De Morgan = A - (B n C). Checked on a concrete instance: A = {1,2,3}, B = {2,3}, C = {3} gives (A-B) U (A-C) = {1} U {1,2} = {1,2}, and A - (B n C) = A - {3} = {1,2}, while A n (B n C) = {3} and A n (B - C) = {2}.
subtopic: Set Operations, Identities, and Cartesian Products of Sets

working: B = B n (A U B) = B n (A U C) = (B n A) U (B n C) = (A n C) U (B n C) = (A U B) n C = (A U C) n C = C, using both hypotheses. So B = C. A = B and A = C need not hold (take A = {1}, B = C = {2}), and A n B need not be empty.
subtopic: Set Operations, Identities, and Cartesian Products of Sets

working: Reflexive: a divides a for every natural a. Transitive: a|b and b|c imply a|c. Not symmetric: 2|4 but 4 does not divide 2, which also rules out 'equivalence relation'. So reflexive and transitive only.
subtopic: Relations — Properties, Cartesian Product, and Counting

Put x = a-b, y = b-c, z = c-a, so x + y + z = 0 identically. The hypothesis is 2y^2 = x^2 + z^2. From x + z = -y we get x^2 + z^2 = y^2 - 2xz, so 2y^2 = y^2 - 2xz, i.e. y^2 = -2xz, i.e. 2/y = -(y)/(xz) = (x+z)/(xz) = 1/x + 1/z. That is exactly the condition for 1/x, 1/y, 1/z to be in AP, and the step is reversible. Verified numerically with y = 1, x = -(1+sqrt3)/2, z = (sqrt3-1)/2: squares 1.866, 1, 0.134 are in AP and reciprocals -0.732, 1, 2.732 are in AP.

(x-a)(x-b) = c is x^2 - (a+b)x + (ab-c) = 0, so alpha + beta = a+b and alpha*beta = ab-c. Then (x-alpha)(x-beta) + c = x^2 - (a+b)x + (ab-c) + c = x^2 - (a+b)x + ab = (x-a)(x-b), whose roots are a and b.

Let the roots be r and r^2. Product r^3 = 3/3 = 1. r = 1 gives sum 2 = -p/3, i.e. p = -6, inadmissible since p > 0. The other cube roots of unity give roots omega and omega^2 with sum -1 = -p/3, so p = 3. Check: 3x^2 + 3x + 3 = 0 has roots omega, omega^2 and (omega)^2 = omega^2, so one root is indeed the square of the other.
Discriminant = 16 - 8m(m+1) >= 0, i.e. m^2 + m - 2 <= 0, i.e. (m+2)(m-1) <= 0, giving -2 <= m <= 1. Option D is the complementary (wrong-sign) region and A/B are each only half the condition.
subtopic: Nature of Roots and Boundary Conditions

working: alpha + beta = sqrt2, alpha*beta = sqrt3. So alpha^2 + beta^2 = 2 - 2sqrt3, and alpha^4 + beta^4 = (alpha^2+beta^2)^2 - 2(alpha*beta)^2 = (2-2sqrt3)^2 - 2*3 = (16 - 8sqrt3) - 6 = 10 - 8sqrt3 (approx -3.856). Confirmed by evaluating the two (complex) roots directly.

For n >= 5, n! contains both 3 and 5 as factors, so 15 divides n! and those terms contribute nothing. Only 1! + 2! + 3! + 4! = 1 + 2 + 6 + 24 = 33 survives, and 33 mod 15 = 3. Confirmed by summing all 95 factorials exactly and reducing mod 15.
T_n = C(n,3) since any 3 vertices of a convex polygon form a triangle. C(n+1,3) - C(n,3) = C(n,2) = n(n-1)/2 = 21 gives n(n-1) = 42, so n = 7. Checked: C(8,3) - C(7,3) = 56 - 35 = 21.

The six throws must consist of three 2s and three 4s in some order: 6!/(3!3!) = 20 favourable sequences out of 6^6 = 46656 equally likely ones, giving 20/46656 = 5/11664. Enumerated the 20 sequences explicitly to confirm the count.

nC6 / (n-3)C3 = [n!/(6!(n-6)!)] * [3!(n-6)!/(n-3)!] = n(n-1)(n-2) * 3!/6! = n(n-1)(n-2)/120. Setting this equal to 33/4 gives n(n-1)(n-2) = 990 = 11*10*9, so n = 11 (the unique integer solution, checked over n = 6..39).
